# Executive Summary
This report uses 71,913 exact-deduplicated compensation records from an
August 2025 global AI and technology salary dataset to propose a focused
executive-recruiting strategy for Libeccio Executive Search. Our strongest
opportunity is specialist searches for senior machine-learning/AI and
software-platform leaders, with technical product leadership as a secondary
specialty. The data show substantial cross-sectional differences in base pay
by role and experience tier, while a regression of on-site versus fully remote
records finds a small estimated conditional remote-pay difference (−0.7%,
95% CI approximately −1.69% to +0.24%). This estimate does not establish
pay equivalence, a causal effect, or whether a specific role can be remote.

We recommend approaching Walmart Global Tech as a **prospective pilot client**,
not because its internal recruiting team is inadequate, but because its
publicly documented AI and technology initiatives and senior technical job
postings provide a plausible setting for targeted specialist search. Our
salary dataset provides broad market context; Walmart's advertised role- and
location-specific ranges provide a necessary employer-specific check.
The proposed next step is one narrowly scoped search pilot, with a follow-up
compensation study covering geography, bonuses, and equity before quoting
exact total-pay packages or placement-fee forecasts.

# 3 Core Questions

Using our data we aim to answer these core questions:

1.  **How does reported base salary differ by experience tier, from
    Entry through Executive, across technical role families?**

2.  **Is remote status associated with higher or lower reported base pay,
    after accounting for observed role and experience differences?**

3.  **Where do reported salary benchmarks differ by year and company
    size, and what does that imply for choosing a recruiting client?**

**How the questions fit together.** Question 1 identifies the senior role
families for which targeted sourcing may create the most value. Question 2
examines whether reported base salary differs by remote status, while
recognizing that work arrangements and geographic pay policies remain
role-specific. Question 3 evaluates the limits of interpreting employer size
and recent-year patterns, so that we do not mistake patterns in an uneven
survey for verified Walmart hiring needs. Section 4 combines the market
findings with independently sourced Walmart-specific evidence.

# 1. Data Scope and Credibility

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

# Consistent role-family palette across comparisons.
role_palette <- c(
  "Data & BI Analyst" = "#4477AA",
  "Data Engineering & Architecture" = "#228833",
  "Data Scientist" = "#66CCEE",
  "Machine Learning / AI" = "#CC6677",
  "Product & Technical Leadership" = "#AA3377",
  "Software & Platform Engineering" = "#CCBB44"
)
```

```{r load-data, echo=FALSE}
salaries <- read_csv(paste0(
  "https://stat.cmu.edu/~sgallagh/courses/mads-fall-2026/",
  "datavis-36613/data/salaries.csv.gz"
))

access_date <- Sys.Date()

n_rows <- nrow(salaries)
n_cols <- ncol(salaries)

```

## What does one row represent?

Each row is one reported compensation record for a single
job/person-year combination, self-submitted to the aijobs.net survey. It
is not a job posting, not a hire event, and there is no employer name,
posting ID, observation date, or row-level source to verify any
individual record. The raw dataset contains 151,445 observations across
11 variables.

## Exact duplicates

```{r duplicates, echo=FALSE}
# Create the exact-deduplicated analysis sample
salaries_no_duplicates <- salaries |>
  distinct()

# Summarize the duplicate audit
duplicate_audit <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "All supplied records",
    "Exact-deduplicated records",
    "Repeated copies removed",
    "Share removed"
  ),
  value = c(
    comma(nrow(salaries)),
    comma(nrow(salaries_no_duplicates)),
    comma(nrow(salaries) - nrow(salaries_no_duplicates)),
    percent(
      1 - nrow(salaries_no_duplicates) / nrow(salaries),
      accuracy = 0.1
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  duplicate_audit,
  col.names = c("Audit Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "Exact-duplicate audit"
)

# Compare experience-tier medians before and after deduplication
duplicate_sensitivity <- bind_rows(
  salaries |>
    mutate(sample = "All supplied records"),
  salaries_no_duplicates |>
    mutate(sample = "Exact duplicates removed")
) |>
  mutate(
    experience_level = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(sample, experience_level) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    n = comma(n),
    median_salary = dollar(median_salary, accuracy = 1)
  )

knitr::kable(
  duplicate_sensitivity,
  col.names = c("Sample", "Experience Level", "Count (n)", "Median Salary (USD)"),
  caption = "Sensitivity of experience-tier salary medians to duplicate handling"
)

# Set primary analysis sample
salaries_analysis <- salaries_no_duplicates
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    experience_level = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = experience_level, y = salary_in_usd)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2, fill = "slategray2") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported salary rises across experience tiers after exact de-duplication",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Unique exact records only; n = 71,913. Salary is annual nominal USD,",
      "not total compensation or cost-of-living adjusted."
    ),
    x = "Experience level",
    y = "Annual salary in USD (log scale)",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net global salary survey snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Exact duplicates removed."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The dataset contained 151,445 supplied compensation records. Removing
exact duplicate rows left 71,913 unique records, meaning that 52.5% of
supplied rows were repeated copies of an identical record. Because the
archive has no respondent ID, employer name, posting ID, or row-level
provenance, we cannot determine whether those repeated rows are data
duplicates or distinct respondents with identical observed
characteristics. We wanted to prevent potentially repeated observations
from receiving extra weight, and we want to reduce the risk of
overstating the amount of information in the dataset. Therefore, we use
the exact de-duplicated dataset ($n = 71,913$) for our primary analysis.

## Missingness and Currency Standardization

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Missingness audit across all 11 variables
missing_audit <- salaries_analysis |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing_Count") |>
  mutate(Missing_Pct = percent(Missing_Count / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.1))

knitr::kable(
  missing_audit,
  col.names = c("Variable Name", "Missing Values (NA)", "Missing Share"),
  caption = "Field-level missingness audit across deduplicated records (n = 71,913)"
)

# Currency breakdown (Top 5)
currency_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  count(salary_currency, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  currency_summary,
  col.names = c("Currency Code", "Record Count", "Share of Total"),
  caption = "Top reporting currencies prior to USD normalization"
)

```

Across all 11 supplied variables in the deduplicated sample
($n = 71,913$), an explicit missingness audit revealed zero missing
values (`NA = 0`).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Conversion Rate Consistency Check for Top Non-USD Currencies
conversion_rates <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(salary_currency %in% c("EUR", "GBP", "CAD")) |>
  mutate(implied_fx_rate = salary_in_usd / salary) |>
  group_by(work_year, salary_currency) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(implied_fx_rate),
    min_rate = min(implied_fx_rate),
    max_rate = max(implied_fx_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_rate, min_rate, max_rate), ~ round(., 4)))

knitr::kable(
  conversion_rates,
  col.names = c("Work Year", "Currency", "Mean Implied FX", "Min FX", "Max FX"),
  caption = "Implied annual exchange conversion consistency (Local Currency to USD)"
)
```

## Years Covered

```{r year-coverage, echo=FALSE}
year_counts <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(work_year, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  year_counts,
  col.names = c("Work Year", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),

```

The raw dataset spans 2020 through 2025, but density is heavily skewed
toward recent years (2024–2025). An important thing to note is that 2025
will not contain a full calendar year of records as the snapshot was
made in August.

## Countries

```{r geo-coverage, echo=FALSE}
top_employee_countries <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(employee_residence, name = "n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  mutate(
    type = "Employee Residence",
    pct = percent(n / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.01),
    n = comma(n)
  ) %>%
  rename(country_code = employee_residence)

top_company_countries <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(company_location, name = "n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  mutate(
    type = "Company Location",
    pct = percent(n / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.01),
    n = comma(n)
  ) %>%
  rename(country_code = company_location)

geo_combined <- bind_rows(top_employee_countries, top_company_countries) |>
  select(type, country_code, n, pct)

knitr::kable(
  geo_combined,
  col.names = c("Dimension", "Country Code", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Top 5 geographical concentrations for employees and employers"
)
```

The dataset is heavily dominated by US geographic concentration where
83.55% of respondents reside in the United States, and 83.64% of
employing companies are based in the U.S.

## Company size composition

```{r size-composition, echo=FALSE}
company_summary <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(company_size, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    company_size = case_when(
      company_size == "S" ~ "Small (<50 employees)",
      company_size == "M" ~ "Medium (50-250 employees)",
      company_size == "L" ~ "Large (>250 employees)"
    ),
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  company_summary,
  col.names = c("Company Size", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Distribution of records by employing firm size"
)
```

The distribution of company size is heavily dominated by Medium-sized
companies (50-250 employees) accounting for 97.5% of all deduplicated
observations ($n=70,110$). Large-sized companies (\>250 employees)
account for 2.2% ($n=1,588$) and Small-sized companies (\<50 employees)
account for 0.3% ($n=215$).

## Remote-status composition

```{r remote-composition, echo=FALSE}
remote_summary <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(remote_ratio, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    remote_ratio = case_when(
      remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-Site (0% remote)",
      remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid (50% remote)",
      remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully Remote (100% remote)"
    ),
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  remote_summary,
  col.names = c("Remote Policy", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Distribution of records by remote work model"
)
```

`remote_ratio` only takes three values: 0 (on-site), 50 (hybrid), 100
(fully remote) so it lacks detail regarding mandatory in-office days or
flexible hybrid policies. On-site observations dominates the
distribution as it accounts for 75.2% of all deduplicated observations.

## Job title composition

```{r, echo=FALSE}
salaries_analysis <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    title_clean = job_title |> str_to_lower() |> str_squish(),
    role_family = case_when(
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bproduct manager\\b|\\bproduct management\\b|\\bproduct owner\\b|\\bproduct lead\\b")) ~ "Product & Technical Leadership",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata scientist\\b|\\bdata science\\b|\\bdecision scientist\\b|\\bcientista de dados\\b")) ~ "Data Scientist",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bmachine learning\\b|\\bml engineer\\b|\\bml scientist\\b|\\bml researcher\\b|\\bmlops\\b|\\bartificial intelligence\\b|\\bai engineer\\b|\\bai architect\\b|\\bai scientist\\b|\\bgenai\\b|\\bcomputer vision\\b|\\bnlp engineer\\b|\\bllm engineer\\b|\\bdeep learning\\b")) ~ "Machine Learning / AI",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata engineer\\b|\\banalytics engineer\\b|\\bdata architect\\b|\\bdata platform\\b|\\bdata infrastructure\\b|\\bdata pipeline\\b|\\bdataops\\b|\\betl\\b")) ~ "Data Engineering & Architecture",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata analyst\\b|\\bbusiness analyst\\b|\\bproduct analyst\\b|\\binsight analyst\\b|\\bbusiness intelligence\\b|\\bbi\\b|\\btableau\\b|\\bpower bi\\b")) ~ "Data & BI Analyst",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bsoftware\\b|\\bsystems? engineer\\b|\\bplatform engineer\\b|\\bdevops\\b|\\bbackend\\b|\\bfrontend\\b|\\bfull[ -]?stack\\b|\\bcloud engineer\\b")) ~ "Software & Platform Engineering",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata manager\\b|\\bengineering manager\\b|\\bdirector of data\\b|\\bhead of data\\b|\\btechnical project manager\\b")) ~ "Product & Technical Leadership",
      TRUE ~ "Other / unclassified"
    )
  )

role_family_table <- salaries_analysis |>
  count(role_family, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  role_family_table,
  col.names = c("Role Family", "Record Count (n)", "Share of Sample"),
  caption = "Standardized role family categorization logic summary"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
role_family_counts <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified") |>
  count(role_family, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    prop = n / sum(n),
    role_family = fct_reorder(role_family, prop)
  )

role_family_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop, y = role_family)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percent(prop, accuracy = 0.1), " (n = ", comma(n), ")")),
    hjust = -0.05,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(
    title = "Role-family representation in the analytic sample",
    subtitle = "Share of exact-deduplicated records with a classified role family.",
    x = "Share of classified records",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary survey (Aug 3, 2025). Exact duplicates removed; unclassified titles excluded."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

The six explicit role families contain **44,439 of 71,913**
exact-deduplicated records (**61.8%**). The remaining **27,474 records
(38.2%)** have an unclassified title. We deliberately leave general titles
such as Engineer, Manager, Analyst, Developer, Director, and Research
Scientist unclassified when the available title alone does not identify
a functional specialty; this is preferable to inventing unsupported
role labels. The classification therefore supports *comparisons among
clearly identified roles*, not conclusions about the entire technology
workforce. Unclassified titles remain in analyses that do not use role
family; the regression appendix also provides a sensitivity check that
retains them as their own category. A future iteration could audit the most
frequent unclassified titles and incorporate verified job-description data.

### Audit of unclassified job titles

The most common unclassified titles are listed below to make the
classification decision auditable. Some may deserve reassignment only
after checking verified job descriptions; an unknown title is not
automatically a low-skilled or unrelated role.

```{r unclassified-title-audit, echo=FALSE}
salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family == "Other / unclassified") |>
  count(job_title, sort = TRUE, name = "n") |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Unclassified Job Title", "Record Count"),
    caption = "Most frequent titles left outside the six specific role families"
  )
```

## Cross-border sparsity

```{r cross-border-sparsity, echo=FALSE}
cross_border_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    geography_type = if_else(
      employee_residence == company_location,
      "Domestic (Same Country)",
      "Cross-Border (Remote International)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(geography_type) |>
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.2),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  cross_border_summary,
  col.names = c("Geographic Relationship", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Comparison of domestic vs. cross-border employment arrangements"
)
```

Cross-border records (where employee residence is not the same as
company location) were too sparse to support robust geographic-arbitrage
modeling. Only 156 of 71,913 unique records (0.2%) represent
cross-border employment relationships.

## Audit limits

-   Removing exact duplicates reduced the dataset from 151,445 to 71,913
    records (a 52.5% reduction). Without respondent or posting
    identifiers, we cannot confirm whether the repeats were data
    duplication or distinct people with identical observed value.

-   The archive has no employer name, posting ID, observation date, or
    row-level source to verify individual entries.

-   Record counts represent survey submissions, not employer demand or
    job-opening counts.

-   \`salary_in_usd\` reflects nominal base salary only, not total
    compensation, and is unadjusted for inflation or local purchasing
    power.

-   Remote status is limited to three discrete values (0, 50, 100)
    without detail on hybrid policies.

-   Employee residence and employer location are recorded at the country
    level, omitting city- or regional-level variation.

-   Cross-border employer/employee pairs (0.22% of unique records) are
    too sparse for reliable comparison.

-   All observed differences across roles, experience levels, and
    company sizes are descriptive associations only.

-   The data source also has the majority of salary observations in 2024
    to 2025. This means that there are limited time series analysis
    opportunities.

# 2. Compensation landscape

**From data quality to an actionable benchmark.** Because the records are
self-reported, strongly concentrated in a subset of years and employer
sizes, and contain unusually high salaries, medians and interquartile
ranges offer a more defensible first comparison than arithmetic means.
We first establish which role families sit toward the upper end of the
reported salary distribution, then investigate whether experience tier
and work arrangement change that comparison.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
family_audit <- salaries_analysis |>
  group_by(role_family) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    share = n / nrow(salaries_analysis),
    unique_titles = n_distinct(job_title),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_salary))

family_audit |>
  mutate(
    share = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n),
    unique_titles = comma(unique_titles),
    across(
      c(median_salary, lower_quartile, upper_quartile),
      ~ dollar(.x, accuracy = 1)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Role Family", "Count (n)", "Share", "Unique Titles", "Median Salary", "25th Percentile", "75th Percentile"),
    caption = "Coverage and compensation summaries under the final role-family rules (deduplicated sample)"
  )
```

## The Compensation Distribution & Outlier Dashboard

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Identify high earners for annotation
high_earner_threshold <- 500000

salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = salary_in_usd, y = fct_reorder(role_family, salary_in_usd, median), fill = role_family)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "slategray", outlier.alpha = 0.2, outlier.size = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = role_palette) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = high_earner_threshold, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 470000, y = 0.8,
    label = "Extreme threshold: $500k+",
    color = "firebrick", hjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = label_dollar(),
    breaks = c(30000, 100000, 300000, 500000, 1000000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "High-Tier Compensation Variance and Extreme Outliers Across Role Domains",
    subtitle = "Log10 scale boxplots isolating extreme compensation outliers (≥ $500,000 threshold).",
    x = "Annual Reported Base Salary in Nominal USD (log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Deduplicated analytic sample."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

Across the deduplicated sample ($n = 71,913$), reported base salaries
displayed right-skewness and extreme high-end outliers across all
technical categories. Therefore, we decided to use medians and
interquartile ranges (IQR) as the primary metrics for central tendency
and spread.

Machine Learning / AI displayed the highest median reported salary at
\$170,042 ($n = 6,144$, 8.5% of sample; IQR: \$125,375–\$226,000).
Product & Technical Leadership at \$163,925 ( $n = 3,381$, 4.7%; IQR: \$114,500–\$224,000) and
Software & Platform Engineering at \$159,000 ( $n = 8,149$, 11.3%; IQR: \$117,000–\$210,985)
follow closely as top-tier compensation drivers. Data Scientist roles
report a median salary of \$142,000 ($n = 7,356$, 10.2%; IQR:
\$100,000–\$191,500), closely followed by Data Engineering &
Architecture at \$139,400 ($n = 9,903$, 13.8%; IQR: \$99,800–\$186,000).
Data & BI Analyst records the lowest compensation baseline among defined
role families at \$100,000 ($n = 9,506$, 13.2%; IQR:
\$72,500–\$136,000), with a difference of \$70,042 from the ML/AI median
(a 41.2% lower baseline).

# 3. Career and market signals

## Client Question 1: How do compensation trajectories differ across career levels, and what is the financial return when progressing through tiers?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Summarize salary medians by role family and experience level
role_experience_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified") |>
  group_by(role_family, experience_level) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    experience_level = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")
    )
  )

# Calculate adjacent-tier dollar and percentage progression
career_progression <- role_experience_summary |>
  arrange(role_family, experience_level) |>
  group_by(role_family) |>
  mutate(
    previous_level = lag(experience_level),
    previous_median = lag(median_salary),
    dollar_increase = median_salary - previous_median,
    percent_increase = 100 * (median_salary - previous_median) / previous_median
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
role_experience_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = experience_level, y = median_salary, color = role_family, group = role_family)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = role_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported salary rises across career tiers in every role family",
    subtitle = "Median annual reported base salary by experience tier and role family.",
    x = "Experience Tier",
    y = "Median Base Salary (USD)",
    color = "Role Family",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary survey (Aug 3, 2025). Exact duplicates removed."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

```

The line chart compares **separate groups of workers**, not the
compensation changes of the same people over time. Reported medians
increase with experience tier across all six classified role families,
and senior/executive roles are especially relevant for a specialist
search practice. However, the gaps should not be described as actual
promotion raises, expected career returns, or firm-specific offer
budgets. The priority-role benchmark table in Section 4 supplies the
corresponding sample sizes and exact SE/EX medians.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
career_progression |>
  filter(!is.na(previous_level)) |>
  mutate(
    transition = factor(
      paste(previous_level, "to", experience_level),
      levels = c("Entry to Mid", "Mid to Senior", "Senior to Executive")
    ),
    role_family = fct_reorder(role_family, percent_increase, .fun = mean)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = transition, y = role_family, fill = percent_increase)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent_increase, 1), "%\n+$", comma(dollar_increase))),
    size = 3.8,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "gray95", high = "steelblue", labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Salary gains between adjacent career tiers vary substantially by role",
    subtitle = "Percentage and dollar differences between adjacent median salary levels.",
    x = "Adjacent Tier Transition",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Percent Difference",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary survey (Aug 3, 2025). Compares separate experience groups, not longitudinal raises."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

This plot displays a heatmap matrix mapping role families against
adjacent career tier transitions. Each cell displays both the percentage
salary difference and the absolute dollar gain, shaded by the magnitude
of the percentage increase. Engineering & Architecture yields the
highest early-career (Entry to Mid) promotion gain at +48.5%
(+$\$38,800$), followed by Data Scientist at +36.2% (+$\$32,001$). Data
Scientist leads mid-career (Mid to Senior) progression with a +32.8%
(+$\$39,549$) median step-up. Lastly, Data Engineering & Architecture
records the largest absolute executive expansion at +30.0%
(+$\$45,000$), followed by Data and BI Analyst at +23% (+$\$27,056$) and
Data Science Leadership at +18.9% (+$\$30,250$).

### Key findings

Differences between experience groups vary by role family: the largest
*percentage* step-up need not belong to the field with the highest
*absolute* executive pay. Thus we should choose search priorities using
both observed senior/executive compensation levels and evidence of
client-specific business need, rather than using the heatmap to infer
promotion budgets. This motivates the next question: whether expanding
the sourcing geography would necessarily require a different pay band.

## Client Question 2: Is there a measurable remote work premium or remote penalty?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
remote_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = case_when(
      remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-site",
      remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid",
      remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully remote"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(remote_status) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    share = n() / nrow(salaries_analysis),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n),
    across(c(median_salary, lower_quartile, upper_quartile), ~ dollar(., accuracy = 1))
  )

knitr::kable(
  remote_summary,
  col.names = c("Remote Status", "Count (n)", "Share", "Median Salary", "25th Percentile", "75th Percentile"),
  caption = "Unadjusted salary statistics by remote work arrangement"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = factor(
      case_when(
        remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-site",
        remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid",
        remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully remote"
      ),
      levels = c("On-site", "Hybrid", "Fully remote")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = remote_status, y = salary_in_usd, fill = remote_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_dollar()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("slategray2", "goldenrod2", "steelblue3")) +
  labs(
    title = "Raw salary distributions overlap across remote work arrangements",
    subtitle = "Unadjusted comparisons do not control for role mix, seniority, firm size, or work year.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Annual Base Salary in Nominal USD (log scale)",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Deduplicated sample."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The plot shows a side-by-side boxplot display and accompanying summary
table comparing reported annual base salary distributions in nominal USD
(on a log scale) across three remote work categories: On-site (0%),
Hybrid (50%), and Fully Remote (100%). Fully Remote roles report an
unadjusted median base salary of $\$140,000$ (IQR:
$\$100,000$–$\$187,200$), closely matching On-site roles at $\$138,300$
(IQR: $\$95,300$–$\$192,890$). Hybrid roles represent a sparse,
lower-paid subset (0.5% of records, $\$69,999$ median). Raw comparisons
fail to show a clear difference between the distributions of on-site and
fully remote salaries but justifies the need for multiple regression.

### Regression Analysis

To estimate the conditional association between remote status and
reported base salary, we fit a log-linear model controlling for role
family, experience level, company size, and work year. We take the natural log of salaries in order to satisfy
linear assumptions, as the salary distribution appears severely
right-skewed and heteroskedastic (see [Appendix](#appendix)). Our main
covariate of interest is remote status as we want to determine whether
remote employees face a compensation premium. The model controls for the
other potential confounding variables including role family controlling
for pay variation across different fields, experience level controlling
for difference in pay depending on seniority, company size controlling
for wage premiums based on small, medium, and large companies, and
lastly work year controlling for changing environmental factors over
time. The primary model compares on-site with fully remote records within
six explicitly classified role families. We initially set aside hybrid
records because only 327 of the 71,913 deduplicated records are coded as
hybrid, and the main question is the on-site versus fully remote
contrast. This restriction makes the coefficient easier to interpret
but may introduce selection bias. Below, a sensitivity model includes
hybrid workers and the unclassified role family rather than assuming
that their exclusion has no effect. Categorical predictors are encoded
with dummy variables.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
remote_model_data <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(
    remote_ratio %in% c(0, 100),
    role_family != "Other / unclassified"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = factor(if_else(remote_ratio == 0, "On-site", "Fully remote"), levels = c("On-site", "Fully remote")),
    experience_level = factor(experience_level, levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"), labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")),
    company_size = factor(company_size, levels = c("S", "M", "L"), labels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large")),
    work_year = factor(work_year)
  )

remote_salary_model <- lm(
  log(salary_in_usd) ~ remote_status + role_family + experience_level + company_size + work_year,
  data = remote_model_data
)

# Lecture-native regression summary conversion using base R coef()
model_coefs <- summary(remote_salary_model)$coefficients |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "Term") |>
  mutate(
    `Estimate (log)` = round(Estimate, 4),
    `Implied % Change` = percent(exp(Estimate) - 1, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Std. Error` = round(`Std. Error`, 4),
    `p-value` = if_else(`Pr(>|t|)` < 0.001, "< 0.001", as.character(round(`Pr(>|t|)`, 3)))
  ) |>
  select(Term, `Estimate (log)`, `Implied % Change`, `Std. Error`, `p-value`)

knitr::kable(
  head(filter(model_coefs, Term != "(Intercept)"), 10),
  caption = "Log-linear salary regression model coefficients (selected key variables)"
)
```

Holding role family, experience tier, company size, and work year constant, fully remote status exhibits an estimated coefficient of $\hat{\beta} = -0.0073$, corresponding to an implied salary difference of -0.7% compared to on-site roles.
This coefficient is statistically insignificant ($t = -1.47, p = 0.141$). The 95% confidence interval for the remote status coefficient ranges from -1.69% to +0.24%. Because zero is included in this interval and the $p$-value exceeds $\alpha = 0.05$, we fail to reject the null hypothesis of equal pay.
By contrast, experience tier and role family show much larger estimated conditional pay associations. In the fitted model, Executive records have an estimated **+90.4%** difference ($\hat{\beta} = 0.6439, p < 0.001$) relative to Entry-level records, while Machine Learning / AI has a **+50.5%** estimated difference ($\hat{\beta} = 0.4086, p < 0.001$) over the Data & BI Analyst baseline.

### Sensitivity check: hybrid workers and unclassified roles

The instructor's feedback raises a reasonable concern: excluding hybrid
workers and generic job titles could change the adjusted association.
We therefore compare the original two-group model with a second model
that retains all three remote categories and the unclassified role
family. A third model restricts the original comparison to US-resident
workers at US-based employers, closer to the proposed Walmart use case.
In all models, *On-site* remains the reference group; the reported
coefficient is the fully remote versus on-site contrast.

```{r remote-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
remote_all_data <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(salary_in_usd > 0) |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = factor(
      case_when(
        remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-site",
        remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid",
        remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully remote"
      ),
      levels = c("On-site", "Hybrid", "Fully remote")
    ),
    experience_level = factor(experience_level, levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX")),
    company_size = factor(company_size, levels = c("S", "M", "L")),
    work_year = factor(work_year)
  )

remote_all_model <- lm(
  log(salary_in_usd) ~ remote_status + role_family +
    experience_level + company_size + work_year,
  data = remote_all_data
)

remote_us_data <- remote_model_data |>
  filter(employee_residence == "US", company_location == "US")

remote_us_model <- lm(
  log(salary_in_usd) ~ remote_status + role_family +
    experience_level + company_size + work_year,
  data = remote_us_data
)

summarize_remote_coefficient <- function(model, label) {
  term <- "remote_statusFully remote"
  beta <- unname(coef(model)[term])
  ci <- confint(model, parm = term)
  tibble(
    Model = label,
    N = comma(nobs(model)),
    `Adjusted remote difference` = percent(exp(beta) - 1, accuracy = 0.1),
    `95% CI, low` = percent(exp(ci[1]) - 1, accuracy = 0.1),
    `95% CI, high` = percent(exp(ci[2]) - 1, accuracy = 0.1)
  )
}

bind_rows(
  summarize_remote_coefficient(remote_salary_model, "Classified, on-site vs fully remote"),
  summarize_remote_coefficient(remote_all_model, "All roles and all remote categories"),
  summarize_remote_coefficient(remote_us_model, "US-to-US, classified, on-site vs fully remote")
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Sensitivity of adjusted fully remote versus on-site salary estimate")
```

### Key findings

In the primary specification, the fully remote coefficient is small
(−0.7%) and its confidence interval includes zero. This does **not**
prove that salaries are equivalent or that remote recruiting requires
no additional compensation. The sensitivity table shows whether the
estimate changes when omitted groups are retained. Any nationwide
sourcing recommendation must also consider occupation, candidate
location, the position's permitted work arrangements, and Walmart's
published location-specific compensation bands.

career_size_summary |>

The heatmap compares reported base-salary medians by company-size
category and experience tier. Medium-sized employers show a higher
executive median ($190,000) than large employers ($140,973) in **this
sample**, but 97.5% of the deduplicated observations come from the
medium category and just 2.2% from the large category. Consequently,
these differences may reflect uneven coverage, occupation mix, or other
unobserved variables. The chart cannot establish that mid-sized
companies have greater willingness to pay, or that these are suitable
compensation bands for Walmart, which belongs to a much larger and
different employer group. Cell labels now show the relevant n.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
year_role_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified", work_year %in% c(2024, 2025)) |>

  summarise(
    n = n(),

year_role_summary |>
  mutate(

    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = work_year_label, y = median_salary, color = role_family, group = role_family)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = role_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported role-family medians differ between full 2024 and partial 2025",
    subtitle = "Separate yearly samples: full-year 2024 versus partial 2025, not worker-level changes.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median Base Salary (USD)",
    color = "Role Family",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). 2025 represents an incomplete calendar year."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +

```

This chart compares *two groups of records*—all of 2024 and only the
portion of 2025 present by August 3. It is not a longitudinal panel of
workers or employers. Product & Technical Leadership has a higher
reported 2025 median than in 2024, whereas several other families are
lower, but shifts in occupation, geography, company size, or response
composition could explain these patterns. They should therefore be
presented as tentative survey benchmarks, not definitive evidence of
salary inflation, market-wide cooling, or accelerating hiring demand.

### Key findings

The company-size and year comparisons are useful for generating
hypotheses, but their uneven sample composition prevents strong claims
about the most profitable clients or fastest-growing hiring markets.
To choose a particular client, we need evidence outside the salary
archive: documented technology priorities, recognizable senior openings,
and location-specific posted compensation. We now apply that standard
to a potential Walmart Global Tech pitch.

# 4. Recruiting Playbook

## Target Employer: Why Walmart Global Tech?

**Why this client, rather than a generic large corporation?** Walmart
is investing in technology-intensive capabilities with direct links to
our salary analysis: AI, software platforms, supply-chain systems, and
e-commerce. Its [FY2026 Form 10-K](https://stock.walmart.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0000104169-26-000055/wmt-20260131.htm)
reports \$16.468 billion of U.S. capital expenditures in a *combined*
category comprising supply chain, customer-facing initiatives,
technology, and other items. This supports the scale of the operational
investment, but is **not** a stand-alone technology budget or evidence
of a specific executive-search contract.

**What indicates potential searches?** The following Walmart career
postings were consulted in October 2026, after the 2025 salary snapshot.
Walmart's publicly advertised
[Group Director, Software Engineering — Applied AI](https://careers.walmart.com/us/en/jobs/R-2599274)
role describes leadership across foundational models, machine-learning
teams, and commercial applications such as search, advertising, and
supply-chain forecasting. The advertised annual **base-pay bands** are
\$195,000–\$370,000 in Bentonville and \$254,000–\$481,000 in Sunnyvale.
A separate [Director, Software Engineering](https://careers.walmart.com/us/en/jobs/R-2640730)
posting lists \$130,000–\$260,000 in Bentonville and \$169,000–\$338,000
in Sunnyvale. These are employer-posted ranges, **not** observed pay,
hire counts, or measured recruiting difficulty; listings may change.
They demonstrate that Walmart recruits for the kinds of senior,
location-sensitive roles relevant to Libeccio's proposed specialty.

**Why might an outside search firm add value despite Walmart's internal
recruiting organization?** We should not argue that Walmart's recruiters
lack executive-search skills without evidence. A more defensible
proposition is *complementary specialization*: Libeccio could undertake
one agreed-upon hard-to-source senior AI or platform leadership search,
research passive candidates across technology markets, compare
location-specific compensation expectations, and deliver a qualified
shortlist. The Bentonville-versus-Sunnyvale pay bands highlight a
practical challenge for offer strategy; they do **not** imply Walmart
permits every role to be fully remote or that a national candidate
search will preserve the same salary budget.

**What would earn the business?** Start with a limited-scope pilot,
subject to confirmation that Walmart has an unmet recruiting need and
is willing to use an external firm. Define the target role, work
location, compensation package, passive-candidate profile, outreach
coverage, and measurable shortlist or time-to-fill outcomes before
negotiating an ongoing relationship. Our salary study helps frame
questions for this pitch, while the Walmart-specific sources establish
why the prospect deserves further consideration. It does not establish
that Walmart has agreed to engage Libeccio or needs an external recruiter.

## Priority Roles and Experience Tiers

Our proposed **primary specialty** is senior and executive ML/AI and
software-platform leadership. These are related capabilities rather
than three unrelated recruiting businesses: applied AI requires both
model-building expertise and the engineering platforms needed to
operate systems reliably at scale. Product & Technical Leadership is
an adjacent, selective specialty where Walmart's specific open roles
call for it. Data Engineering & Architecture is a supporting talent
pipeline worth evaluating because of its relevance to platform and
supply-chain data systems.

The archive's overall medians are \$170,042 for Machine Learning / AI,
\$159,000 for Software & Platform Engineering, and \$163,925 for Product
& Technical Leadership. More relevant to the proposed search niche,
the **executive-tier** median within these groups is \$203,350,
\$193,490, and \$205,050 respectively, with sample sizes of 152,
187, and 316. These are descriptive medians across the full dataset,
not exact estimates of what Walmart should offer. Employer location,
responsibility, equity, and bonuses must be evaluated independently.

## Salary Benchmarks

These metrics summarize annual base salaries across Libeccio’s target
roles.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Directional Compensation Benchmarks for Priority Target Roles
priority_benchmarks <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(
    role_family %in% c(
      "Product & Technical Leadership",
      "Machine Learning / AI",
      "Software & Platform Engineering"
    ),
    experience_level %in% c("SE", "EX")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    experience_tier = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Senior", "Executive")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(role_family, experience_tier) |>
  summarise(
    sample_size = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(role_family, experience_tier) |>
  mutate(
    sample_size = comma(sample_size),
    across(c(median_salary, q25, q75), ~ dollar(., accuracy = 1))
  )

knitr::kable(
  priority_benchmarks,
  col.names = c("Role Family", "Experience Tier", "Sample Size (n)", "Median Base Salary", "25th Percentile", "75th Percentile"),
  caption = "Directional Compensation Benchmarks for Target Sourcing Priorities (Source: aijobs.net frozen snapshot, Aug. 3, 2025; deduplicated N = 71,913)"
)
```

In the generated benchmark table, median Senior-tier base salaries
range from **\$172,625 to \$184,000**, and median Executive-tier base
salaries range from **\$193,490 to \$205,050** across the three proposed
families. The subgroup sample sizes, especially in the Executive tier,
should accompany these figures. These are directional survey medians,
not evidence of Walmart's actual offers, total compensation, or
recruiter placement fees; Walmart's published location-specific
job bands offer an additional, employer-specific reference.

## Search Strategy

Libeccio should **offer Walmart a tightly scoped pilot search** focused
on one senior AI / machine-learning or platform-engineering leadership
position. Begin by confirming the role's business owner, location and
work-arrangement requirements, essential skills, reporting scope,
compensation structure, and whether outside sourcing is desired.

The immediate deliverable would be a market map of relevant talent,
compensation comparisons segmented by geography and seniority, and a
shortlist of qualified candidates who meet the agreed criteria. A
successful pilot could create an opening for adjacent product or data
engineering searches, but longer-term client value and repeat business
should be framed as goals rather than guaranteed outcomes.

Use the **survey's role/experience medians to set initial research
questions**, and Walmart's advertised bands and validated
bonus/equity benchmarks to determine actual offer competitiveness.
Reject claims about automatic remote-pay savings, fixed placement fee
margins, or which roles are definitively most profitable: those require
information that the current dataset does not contain.

## Next Data Source

The compensation archive contains annual nominal base salary but not
restricted stock units, annual bonuses, sign-on awards, or other forms
of compensation. A next-stage offer study should obtain a consistent
source of total-compensation benchmarks (for example, Pave, Levels.fyi,
or an employer-sponsored compensation survey), verify the methodology
and licensing terms, and combine it with role- and location-specific
Walmart salary bands. Only then could Libeccio build credible offer
scenarios or negotiate a placement-fee structure grounded in the
expected scope of the search.

**Bottom line:** the evidence supports a targeted *prospective-client
pitch* and an AI/platform leadership search hypothesis—not a claim that
Walmart has a recruiting deficiency, that remote pay is universally
identical, or that the archive measures hiring demand.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
remote_reduced_model <- lm(
  log(salary_in_usd) ~ role_family + experience_level + company_size + factor(work_year),
  data = remote_model_data
)

anova(remote_reduced_model, remote_salary_model)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
est <- coef(remote_salary_model)["remote_statusFully remote"]
ci  <- confint(remote_salary_model, "remote_statusFully remote")
exp(est) - 1
exp(ci) - 1
```

## Reproducibility and analytical decisions

- **Source data:** [Course-hosted aijobs.net salary CSV](https://stat.cmu.edu/~sgallagh/courses/mads-fall-2026/datavis-36613/data/salaries.csv.gz); reported salary snapshot through August 3, 2025. Rechecked when the report is rendered: `r format(access_date, "%Y-%m-%d")`. The remote host could change; save a permitted versioned data copy or checksum for archival reproducibility.
- **Unit:** One salary record in the supplied archive. This is neither a verified unique employee nor a posted job opening.
- **Cleaning:** `distinct()` across all 11 supplied columns removes exact duplicate records (151,445 to 71,913); it cannot identify unique people. Role-family assignment uses ordered title-based keyword rules shown in the source code; unknown roles are not silently imputed.
- **Salary measure:** `salary_in_usd`, nominal annual base salary, not cost-of-living adjusted and not total pay. Reported local-currency conversions are checked descriptively, not re-estimated.
- **Inference:** The main remote model compares on-site and fully remote classified records; the sensitivity model retains hybrid and unclassified rows. Neither model identifies a causal effect or controls for city-level geography.
- **Limitations:** Large-company, hybrid, cross-border, executive subgroups, and 2025 partial-year comparisons require special caution. External Walmart descriptions are sourced separately from the salary survey and must be revalidated when job postings change.
